title: Object-Relational Model
description: Compare relational foundations with composite values, arrays, inheritance, and semi-structured columns, using labeled PostgreSQL examples and MySQL mirrors with explicit verification limits.
notes:
## Extending a relational foundation

The object-relational model retains relations and SQL while adding facilities that can represent richer values or type relationships. Composite types, collections, specialized types, and inheritance-related features are common examples discussed in this family. Products support different combinations, so object-relational is not a universal syntax specification or a promise that every extension behaves like a programming-language class.

PostgreSQL is a familiar example used to illustrate several such capabilities. This course otherwise uses MySQL 8.4 for executable SQL practice. PostgreSQL snippets below are explicitly labeled comparisons, and the MySQL exercises represent selected query ideas with ordinary tables. A successful mirror query does not verify PostgreSQL inheritance or composite-type execution.

The key design question is which facts and operations benefit from a richer representation without losing clear identity, validity rules, and query meaning. Adding a complex column is not automatically an improvement, and retaining tables does not automatically guarantee every transaction or authorization property. Those contracts still require the selected engine and implementation.

## Distinguishing values from entity identity

A customer can have a structured address value containing street, city, and postal code. That value may be useful as one typed component, but it is not necessarily an independently identified entity. Two customers can have equal address values without becoming the same customer or sharing one authoritative mutable address object.

By contrast, a persistent object model often emphasizes object identity and references. Object-relational extensions can coexist with ordinary table keys and SQL relationships. Do not infer that a composite field automatically has an OID, methods, or an independent lifecycle. The type definition tells us how the value is structured; entity identity needs its own contract.

The same distinction applies to updates. Replacing one customer's address value need not change another customer's equal value. If the domain instead requires a shared address record, model that sharing explicitly. A nested-looking representation does not decide ownership merely by placing several field names inside one column.

## Defining a structured value with labeled syntax

PostgreSQL supports composite types whose fields have names and declared types. The following comparison illustrates an original address structure. It is not MySQL syntax and is not executed by the tutorial's SQL mirror exercises.

```sql
-- PostgreSQL comparison only.
CREATE TYPE campus_address AS (
  street text,
  city text,
  postal_code text
);
```

Such a type can be used in supported expression and column contexts. Postal code remains text because leading zeros or nonnumeric labels may matter. The grouping of fields provides a reusable structure, but business rules such as a required city do not follow merely because the field exists.

PostgreSQL composite values also have constraint considerations. Constraints attached to a table using a row type do not automatically become universal constraints on every independent value of that type. Review the actual type and domain facilities when validation must apply outside the original table. Structural typing and valid business states are related but separate concerns.

## Understanding arrays and repeated facts

An array can hold several values in one column under supported engine rules. A phone-number array may be convenient when the task treats a small ordered collection as part of one customer value. It is not necessarily the best model when each phone entry has its own owner, verification history, category, or lifecycle.

Avoid the simplistic claim that every array is automatically a normalization violation with identical consequences. Atomicity depends on the modeled domain and intended operations, while practical design still needs to ask which repeated facts require independent constraints and relationships. A child relation can make per-entry identity and cross-record rules clearer for some requirements.

Performance also depends on the workload. An embedded collection can simplify one retrieval while making other updates, membership queries, or integrity requirements more difficult. Use measured operations and explicit invariants rather than assuming fewer joins always means better design. A compact physical representation is not the same as a complete logical model.

## Examining table inheritance as a product feature

PostgreSQL table inheritance lets a child table inherit columns from a parent under its documented rules. A comparison can define premium_customers using INHERITS customers. A normal query of the parent can include rows stored in descendants, while ONLY can restrict a query to rows stored directly in the parent.

This behavior can surprise a report that assumes the parent name means parent-only physical rows. The intended population must be explicit: all represented customers or only direct parent rows. The query's column list can look identical while the population differs. That is a semantic distinction, not merely a spelling variation.

Do not equate this feature with every SQL standard type-inheritance rule or an application's entire class hierarchy. PostgreSQL's own table inheritance has specific behavior and caveats. A child gaining columns does not imply all indexes, uniqueness, or foreign-key guarantees span the whole hierarchy in the way a developer expects.

## Preserving keys and constraints across populations

A primary key on one table should not be assumed to guarantee global uniqueness across inherited tables. An application may need an additional design to enforce the required identity domain. Two physical rows with equal identifiers can therefore be a real modeling issue rather than proof that the engine violated a guarantee it never supplied.

In the teaching mirror, base and premium customer rows live in separate ordinary tables with local keys. Their identifiers can overlap, so the source kind is part of distinguishing returned occurrences. UNION ALL preserves both rows. An accidental UNION over equal projected values can collapse distinct source occurrences and change a count.

The mirror deliberately exposes that risk without creating native inheritance. It can compare a base-only report to one combining both sources. The SQL tests verify those explicit populations and aggregations, not PostgreSQL's metadata, inheritance enforcement, or migration behavior. Exact native feature checks remain separate work.

## Separating JSON from typed object-relational features

A JSON document column can hold semi-structured values under product-specific validation and query support. PostgreSQL JSONB and MySQL JSON are not interchangeable syntax or implementation promises. They also are not identical to a named composite type or table inheritance merely because the visible data can look nested.

A typed composite declares a known field structure. A document representation can permit variable fields and nested content according to its schema and validation policy. Both need rules for required values, types, and evolution. Choosing JSON to avoid reviewing those requirements can move ambiguity into runtime queries rather than remove it.

Use the actual feature name and dialect when discussing behavior. An example using PostgreSQL JSONB should not be presented as executable MySQL SQL, and a MySQL compatibility test on MariaDB does not verify either product's complete document or inheritance subsystem. Scope the claim to what the test actually exercised.

## Evaluating application mapping and evolution

Richer stored values can reduce some translation work for an application, but the application still needs supported representations, parameter binding, and error handling. A language object containing transient UI state should not be stored wholesale merely because the database accepts a structured value. Determine which facts are authoritative and durable.

Changing a type or inherited structure can affect existing rows, functions, queries, and clients. A new field, altered meaning, or stricter validation rule requires a compatible transition plan. Inspect actual dependencies before changing definitions. A type name remaining unchanged does not prove that consumers still interpret its contents correctly.

Authorization and integrity also remain trusted responsibilities. A caller able to submit a nested address does not automatically have permission to update the customer. An application class hierarchy does not grant database rights. Keep the chosen rich representation separate from the controls that determine who may read or change its facts.

## Choosing the extension for a demonstrated need

Start with the required values, identities, relationships, and queries. Compare a simple relational baseline with a supported extension using representative examples, including missing components, repeated values, overlapping subtype identifiers, and parent-only versus combined populations. Test the actual dialect when its native semantics matter.

Object-relational facilities are useful when they express required structure clearly while preserving reviewable contracts. Keep typed values, entities, arrays, inheritance, and documents distinct, and label implementation-specific behavior precisely. That approach makes richer SQL understandable without pretending a complex column or an inheritance keyword automatically supplies global identity, normalization, or compatible application behavior.

questions.question_text: What characterizes object-relational extensions?
options: They are unrelated, competing paradigms
A relational/SQL foundation with supported richer value or type-related facilities
The Object-Relational model has no tables at all
The Object-Relational model replaced SQL with OQL
questions.explanation: Transaction and security guarantees still depend on the actual implementation.

questions.question_text: Which database system is most commonly cited as the textbook example of an object-relational database?
options: MongoDB
Redis
PostgreSQL
Neo4j
questions.explanation: PostgreSQL originated from the Berkeley POSTGRES project explicitly built to add object-oriented concepts to relational databases.

questions.question_text: In PostgreSQL, what does 'CREATE TABLE premium_customers (...) INHERITS (customers)' demonstrate?
options: A foreign key relationship
Table inheritance, an object-relational extension to the pure relational model
A many-to-many junction table
A materialized view
questions.explanation: INHERITS creates a table inheritance relationship, an OO-style feature layered onto the relational model.

questions.question_text: What is a key behavioral quirk of table inheritance in PostgreSQL that can surprise developers?
options: Child tables cannot have any additional columns
A query on the parent table by default also returns rows from child tables unless ONLY is specified
Inherited tables cannot be indexed
Parent table queries never include child rows
questions.explanation: By default, querying the parent table includes rows from all its child tables; using ONLY customers restricts the query to just the parent table's own rows.

questions.question_text: What should determine whether a phone array or a child relation fits a design?
options: It strictly enforces First Normal Form (1NF)
The modeled value, per-entry relationships, constraints, and required operations
It has no relationship to normalization concepts
It automatically creates a separate join table behind the scenes
questions.explanation: An array is not automatically the same normalization decision in every domain.

questions.question_text: What emphasis distinguishes object-relational designs from object-centered persistence?
options: They are identical; OR is just a marketing term for OO databases
They retain a relational foundation while adding supported extensions
OO databases always run on top of relational engines
OR databases cannot support user-defined types
questions.explanation: This comparison concerns model emphasis rather than a universal claim about physical storage internals.

questions.question_text: What SQL object-relational feature lets you define a structured column type, such as an 'address' with street, city, and zip fields?
options: A composite (user-defined) type
A materialized view
A stored procedure
A trigger
questions.explanation: User-defined composite types let a single column hold a structured value, an object-relational extension to plain scalar columns.

questions.question_text: Is a PostgreSQL JSONB column identical to a composite type or table inheritance?
options: Yes, they are identical mechanisms
No; document values, typed composites, and inheritance have different structures and contracts
No, because PostgreSQL does not actually support JSONB
Yes, because both eliminate the need for SQL entirely
questions.explanation: Nested visual appearance does not make their semantics interchangeable.

questions.question_text: Does an equal structured address value automatically identify the same customer?
options: Yes; every composite is a global key
No; value equality and entity identity are different
Only if the postal code is text
Only if the city is required
questions.explanation: Several entities can have equal component values.

questions.question_text: Why label the PostgreSQL comparison syntax in this MySQL-oriented course?
options: Every database rewrites it automatically
Only the comment color differs
The native feature syntax and behavior are dialect-specific
Labels make execution unnecessary everywhere
questions.explanation: A comparison must not be presented as supported target SQL.

questions.question_text: A PostgreSQL parent query includes descendant rows by default. What can ONLY specify?
options: Include every descendant twice
Drop the child table
Restrict the query to the named parent table's own rows
Make every inherited key global
questions.explanation: ONLY controls the relevant inheritance population.

questions.question_text: An application assumes a parent primary key guarantees uniqueness across every inherited child. What requires review?
options: Only the table name spelling
Only the row display order
Nothing; all inheritance shares every index globally
The actual inheritance key and constraint scope
questions.explanation: Native feature caveats can differ from a class-model intuition.

questions.question_text: Two mirror tables contain equal projected rows from distinct sources. Which combining operation preserves both occurrences?
options: UNION ALL
UNION always preserves duplicates
DISTINCT over every label
An arbitrary LIMIT 1
questions.explanation: Removing duplicates can collapse source occurrences.

questions.question_text: A phone entry needs verification history and its own lifecycle. What representation should be considered?
options: An unreviewed array solely because it uses fewer joins
A separately modeled child fact with suitable identity and rules
A concatenated label with no structure
A database role name
questions.explanation: Independent per-entry facts may need more than embedded value storage.

questions.question_text: A composite value is used outside its original table. What cannot be assumed?
options: That the value has fields
That field types were declared
All table constraints automatically apply to that independent value
That the actual product has documentation
questions.explanation: Structure and constraint scope must be checked separately.

questions.question_text: A JSONB example is copied directly into MySQL. What must adaptation check?
options: Only whether the word JSON appears
Only indentation
Only the number of braces
Supported target types, syntax, and semantics
questions.explanation: Related document features are not identical dialect contracts.

questions.question_text: A new field changes a structured value's meaning. What must compatibility review include?
options: Stored values, queries, functions, and direct consumers
Only whether the type name stayed the same
Only the diagram caption
Only the number of columns in another table
questions.explanation: A stable type label does not prove stable interpretation.

questions.question_text: A SQL mirror combines base and premium rows successfully. What remains unverified?
options: The fixture's combined output
Native PostgreSQL inheritance and constraint behavior
That both ordinary sources were queried
That the query ran on its recorded engine
questions.explanation: The mirror verifies explicit query logic only.

questions.question_text: A client submits a nested address. What does that not establish?
options: That input has a structure
That validation may be required
Authorization to update the referenced customer
That the operation has a caller
questions.explanation: Representation does not grant permission.

questions.question_text: An embedded value speeds one read. What should not be concluded without broader evidence?
options: That the measured read improved
That representation can affect cost
That the task has an access pattern
The extension is best for every update, constraint, and query requirement
questions.explanation: Workload and integrity trade-offs remain specific.

coding_problems.title: Combine base and subtype populations in a SQL mirror
coding_problems.task: Using ordinary MySQL tables, return customer_id, customer_name, source_kind from customers and premium_customers. Label sources base and premium. Preserve every source row, including overlapping local identifiers or equal labels. Order by customer_id then source_kind. This is a manual population mirror, not native table inheritance.
coding_problems.schema_sql:
CREATE TABLE customers (customer_id INT PRIMARY KEY, customer_name VARCHAR(40) NOT NULL, reward_points INT NOT NULL CHECK(reward_points>=0));
CREATE TABLE premium_customers (customer_id INT PRIMARY KEY, customer_name VARCHAR(40) NOT NULL, reward_points INT NOT NULL CHECK(reward_points>=0), tier VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL);
coding_problems.seed_sql: INSERT INTO customers VALUES (10,'Noor',5),(30,'Dev',0); INSERT INTO premium_customers VALUES (20,'Mira',8,'gold');
coding_problems.expected:
customer_id	customer_name	source_kind
10	Noor	base
20	Mira	premium
30	Dev	base
constraints: Keys are local to each source table
Use UNION ALL to retain source occurrences
edge_cases: Same local ID can exist in both sources
An empty source does not hide the other
Equal labels do not merge rows
hints: Project the common fields and a source literal
coding_problems.solution_sql: SELECT customer_id,customer_name,'base' AS source_kind FROM customers UNION ALL SELECT customer_id,customer_name,'premium' AS source_kind FROM premium_customers ORDER BY customer_id,source_kind;
coding_problems.explanation: The explicit union mirrors a combined population while source labels distinguish local identities. It does not verify native inheritance semantics.

validation_cases.seed_sql: INSERT INTO customers VALUES (1,'Sam',5); INSERT INTO premium_customers VALUES (1,'Sam',5,'gold');
validation_cases.expected:
customer_id	customer_name	source_kind
1	Sam	base
1	Sam	premium

coding_problems.title: Compare parent-only and combined summary contracts
coding_problems.task: Return two rows with scope, customer_rows, points_total. For base_only summarize customers. For including_premium summarize every row from customers and premium_customers, preserving repeated projected values with UNION ALL. Use COUNT(*) and SUM(reward_points); an empty population has zero rows and NULL total. Order by scope. This is ordinary SQL population logic, not execution of PostgreSQL ONLY or INHERITS.
coding_problems.schema_sql:
CREATE TABLE customers (customer_id INT PRIMARY KEY, customer_name VARCHAR(40) NOT NULL, reward_points INT NOT NULL CHECK(reward_points>=0));
CREATE TABLE premium_customers (customer_id INT PRIMARY KEY, customer_name VARCHAR(40) NOT NULL, reward_points INT NOT NULL CHECK(reward_points>=0), tier VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL);
coding_problems.seed_sql: INSERT INTO customers VALUES (1,'Noor',5),(2,'Dev',0); INSERT INTO premium_customers VALUES (3,'Mira',8,'gold');
edge_cases: Equal projected point values must not collapse
Empty sources still produce both summary rows
hints: Aggregate a UNION ALL derived population for the combined scope
coding_problems.solution_sql: SELECT 'base_only' AS scope,COUNT(*) AS customer_rows,SUM(reward_points) AS points_total FROM customers UNION ALL SELECT 'including_premium' AS scope,COUNT(*) AS customer_rows,SUM(reward_points) AS points_total FROM (SELECT reward_points FROM customers UNION ALL SELECT reward_points FROM premium_customers) x ORDER BY scope;
coding_problems.explanation: The summaries deliberately use different populations. UNION ALL inside the combined population retains equal-valued occurrences, and SUM preserves an empty total as NULL.

validation_cases.expected:
scope	customer_rows	points_total
base_only	0	NULL
including_premium	0	NULL

validation_cases.seed_sql: INSERT INTO customers VALUES (1,'Sam',5); INSERT INTO premium_customers VALUES (1,'Sam',5,'gold');

original_questions.question_text: What is the fundamental relationship between the Object-Relational model and the pure relational model?
options: They are unrelated, competing paradigms
The Object-Relational model extends the relational model with OO features while keeping tables, SQL, and ACID transactions
The Object-Relational model has no tables at all
The Object-Relational model replaced SQL with OQL
original_questions.explanation: The object-relational model is an evolutionary extension of the relational model, adding features like composite types and inheritance while retaining tables and SQL.

original_questions.question_text: Which database system is most commonly cited as the textbook example of an object-relational database?
options: MongoDB
Redis
PostgreSQL
Neo4j
original_questions.explanation: PostgreSQL originated from the Berkeley POSTGRES project explicitly built to add object-oriented concepts to relational databases.

original_questions.question_text: In PostgreSQL, what does 'CREATE TABLE premium_customers (...) INHERITS (customers)' demonstrate?
options: A foreign key relationship
Table inheritance, an object-relational extension to the pure relational model
A many-to-many junction table
A materialized view
original_questions.explanation: INHERITS creates a table inheritance relationship, an OO-style feature layered onto the relational model.

original_questions.question_text: What is a key behavioral quirk of table inheritance in PostgreSQL that can surprise developers?
options: Child tables cannot have any additional columns
A query on the parent table by default also returns rows from child tables unless ONLY is specified
Inherited tables cannot be indexed
Parent table queries never include child rows
original_questions.explanation: By default, querying the parent table includes rows from all its child tables; using ONLY customers restricts the query to just the parent table's own rows.

original_questions.question_text: How does storing a 'phone_numbers text[]' array column directly in a customers table relate to normalization?
options: It strictly enforces First Normal Form (1NF)
It is a deliberate denormalization, trading strict atomicity of values for fewer joins
It has no relationship to normalization concepts
It automatically creates a separate join table behind the scenes
original_questions.explanation: Storing multiple values in one array column is a deliberate deviation from strict 1NF (atomic values only) for convenience and fewer joins.

original_questions.question_text: How does the Object-Relational model differ from the pure Object-Oriented model (3.4)?
options: They are identical; OR is just a marketing term for OO databases
OR databases remain fundamentally table/SQL-based with OO extensions, while OO databases use objects with OIDs as the fundamental storage unit with no underlying tables
OO databases always run on top of relational engines
OR databases cannot support user-defined types
original_questions.explanation: The Object-Relational model keeps the relational foundation (tables, SQL) and adds OO features, whereas the pure OO model discards tables in favor of objects and OIDs as the storage unit.

original_questions.question_text: What SQL object-relational feature lets you define a structured column type, such as an 'address' with street, city, and zip fields?
options: A composite (user-defined) type
A materialized view
A stored procedure
A trigger
original_questions.explanation: User-defined composite types let a single column hold a structured value, an object-relational extension to plain scalar columns.

original_questions.question_text: Is adding a JSONB column to a PostgreSQL table the same thing as using its object-relational features like composite types and table inheritance?
options: Yes, they are identical mechanisms
No — JSONB is a semi-structured, schema-flexible column closer in spirit to the document model, while composite types/inheritance are schema-level, typed object-relational features
No, because PostgreSQL does not actually support JSONB
Yes, because both eliminate the need for SQL entirely
original_questions.explanation: JSONB provides flexible, semi-structured storage (conceptually closer to the document model), whereas true object-relational features like composite types and inheritance are strongly typed and defined at the schema level.
